questions.prompt:
Maya was asked to work out $20 - 4 \times 3$

Maya wrote $20 - 4 = 16$
She then worked out $16 \times 3$

Explain what is wrong with the method.
hints: Think about BIDMAS: which operations come first?
questions.solution:
Model answer: She should do the multiplication before the subtraction. [B1]

Multiplication comes before subtraction: $4 \times 3 = 12$, then $20 - 12 = 8$. Maya subtracted first.
questions.inspiredBy: Edexcel GCSE Maths Foundation Paper 1 (Non-Calculator), November 2024, Q12

questions.prompt:
Sam was asked to work out $12 + 6 \div 3$

Sam wrote $12 + 6 = 18$
He then worked out $18 \div 3 = 6$

Explain what is wrong with the method.
hints: Think about BIDMAS: which operations come first?
questions.solution:
Model answer: He should do the division before the addition. [B1]

Division comes before addition: $6 \div 3 = 2$, then $12 + 2 = 14$. Sam added first.
questions.inspiredBy: Edexcel GCSE Maths Foundation Paper 1 (Non-Calculator), November 2024, Q12

questions.prompt:
Leah was asked to work out $3 \times (8 - 2)$

Leah wrote $3 \times 8 = 24$
She then worked out $24 - 2 = 22$

Explain what is wrong with the method.
hints: Think about BIDMAS: which operations come first?
questions.solution:
Model answer: She should work out the bracket first. [B1]

Brackets come first: $8 - 2 = 6$, then $3 \times 6 = 18$. Leah ignored the bracket.

questions.prompt:
There are 300 people at a party.
$\frac{3}{5}$ of the people are children. The rest of the people are adults.
40% of the children are vegetarian.
25% of the adults are vegetarian.
How many of the people are not vegetarian? (5)
hints: Find the number of children and adults first.
Then find how many of each are vegetarian, and subtract.
questions.solution:
Children: $300 \div 5 \times 3 = 180$, adults: $300 - 180 = 120$ [M1]
Vegetarian children: $40\%$ of $180 = 72$ [M1]
Vegetarian adults: $25\%$ of $120 = 30$ [M1]
Not vegetarian: $(180 - 72) + (120 - 30)$ [M1]
$= 198$ [A1]

questions.prompt:
There are 250 people at a party.
$\frac{2}{5}$ of the people are children. The rest of the people are adults.

50% of the adults are vegetarian.

hints: Find the number of children and adults first.
Then find how many of each are vegetarian, and subtract.
questions.solution:
Children: $250 \div 5 \times 2 = 100$, adults: $250 - 100 = 150$ [M1]
Vegetarian children: $30\%$ of $100 = 30$ [M1]
Vegetarian adults: $50\%$ of $150 = 75$ [M1]
Not vegetarian: $(100 - 30) + (150 - 75)$ [M1]
$= 145$ [A1]

questions.prompt:

questions.prompt:
Amy says that 18 is a square number because $9^2 = 18$
(a) Is the claim correct? Give a reason for your answer. (1)
Chloe says, "When you multiply two odd numbers the answer is always even."
(b) Write down an example to show that Chloe is wrong. (1)
hints: Squaring means multiplying a number by itself, not by 2.
One example that doesn't work (a counterexample) is enough to show a rule is wrong.
questions.solution:
Model answer:
(a) No, because $9^2 = 9 \times 9 = 81$, not 18, and no whole number squared gives 18 ($4^2 = 16$, $5^2 = 25$). [B1]
(b) For example, $3 \times 5 = 15$, which is odd. [B1]

questions.inspiredBy: Edexcel GCSE Maths Foundation Paper 2 (Calculator), November 2024, Q8
questions.prompt:
Ben says that 12 is a cube number because $4^3 = 12$
(a) Is the claim correct? Give a reason for your answer. (1)
Chloe says, "When you add two prime numbers the answer is always even."
(b) Write down an example to show that Chloe is wrong. (1)
hints: Squaring means multiplying a number by itself, not by 2.
One example that doesn't work (a counterexample) is enough to show a rule is wrong.
questions.solution:
Model answer:
(a) No, because $4^3 = 4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$, not 12, and 12 is not a cube number ($2^3 = 8$, $3^3 = 27$). [B1]
(b) For example, $2 + 3 = 5$, which is odd. [B1]

questions.inspiredBy: Edexcel GCSE Maths Foundation Paper 2 (Calculator), November 2024, Q8
questions.prompt:
Cara says that 8 is a square number because $4^2 = 8$
(a) Is the claim correct? Give a reason for your answer. (1)
Chloe says, "An odd number minus an even number is always even."
(b) Write down an example to show that Chloe is wrong. (1)
hints: Squaring means multiplying a number by itself, not by 2.
One example that doesn't work (a counterexample) is enough to show a rule is wrong.
questions.solution:
Model answer:
(a) No, because $4^2 = 16$, not 8, and no whole number squared gives 8 ($2^2 = 4$, $3^2 = 9$). [B1]
(b) For example, $7 - 2 = 5$, which is odd. [B1]

questions.prompt:
(a) Write 180 as a product of its prime factors. (2)
(b) Find the highest common factor (HCF) of 180 and 252 (2)
hints: Use a factor tree: keep splitting until every branch ends in a prime.
The HCF uses the prime factors the two numbers share.
questions.solution:
(a) Factor tree, e.g. $180 = 2 \times 90$… [M1]
$180 = 2^2 × 3^2 × 5$ [A1]

(b) Prime factors of 252: $2\times2\times3\times3\times7$ [M1]
HCF $= 36$ [A1]

questions.inspiredBy: Edexcel GCSE Maths Foundation Paper 3 (Calculator), November 2024, Q23
questions.prompt:
Jana used her calculator to find the value of a number $t$.
The answer on her calculator began 7.4
Complete the error interval for $t$:   ____ $\le t <$ ____ (2)
hints: 'Began' means the rest of the digits were cut off (truncated), not rounded.
So t is at least the number shown, but less than the next value up in the last digit.
questions.solution:
Lower bound: $7.4$ [B1]
Upper bound: $7.5$ (not included), so $7.4 \le t < 7.5$ [B1]

questions.prompt:
Jo uses beads to make necklaces.
For each one she uses 4 blue beads and 9 yellow beads.
Jo has 50 blue beads and 100 yellow beads.
Work out the greatest number of necklaces Jo can make.
You must show all your working. (3)
hints: How many could she make from each colour on its own?
The colour that runs out first decides the answer.
questions.solution:
Blue: $50 \div 4 = 12.5$, so 12 [M1]
Yellow: $100 \div 9 = 11.11$, so 11 [M1]
The greatest number is the smaller: 11 [A1]

questions.inspiredBy: Edexcel GCSE Maths Foundation Paper 2 (Calculator), November 2024, Q6
questions.prompt:
Jo uses beads to make bracelets.
For each one she uses 6 red beads and 5 white beads.
Jo has 75 red beads and 70 white beads.
Work out the greatest number of bracelets Jo can make.
You must show all your working. (3)
hints: How many could she make from each colour on its own?
The colour that runs out first decides the answer.
questions.solution:
Red: $75 \div 6 = 12.5$, so 12 [M1]
White: $70 \div 5 = 14$, so 14 [M1]
The greatest number is the smaller: 12 [A1]

questions.inspiredBy: Edexcel GCSE Maths Foundation Paper 2 (Calculator), November 2024, Q6
questions.prompt:
Jo uses beads to make key rings.
For each one she uses 8 green beads and 3 pink beads.
Jo has 70 green beads and 30 pink beads.
Work out the greatest number of key rings Jo can make.
You must show all your working. (3)
hints: How many could she make from each colour on its own?
The colour that runs out first decides the answer.
questions.solution:
Green: $70 \div 8 = 8.75$, so 8 [M1]
Pink: $30 \div 3 = 10$, so 10 [M1]
The greatest number is the smaller: 8 [A1]

questions.prompt:
1 sandwich and 1 drink cost $\pounds 5.20$
2 sandwiches and 1 drink cost $\pounds 8.70$

Work out the total cost of 3 sandwiches and 2 drinks.
You must show all your working.
hints: Compare the two lines: what is different between them?
The difference in cost is caused only by the extra items.
Once you know one price, use the first line to find the other.
questions.solution:
The extra sandwich costs $\pounds 8.70 - \pounds 5.20 = \pounds 3.50$ [P1]
1 drink $= \pounds 5.20 - \pounds 3.50 = \pounds 1.70$ [P1]
Total: $3 \times \pounds 3.50 + 2 \times \pounds 1.70 = \pounds 10.50 + \pounds 3.40 = \pounds 13.90$ [P1 P1 A1]
questions.inspiredBy: Edexcel GCSE Maths Foundation Paper 1 (Non-Calculator), November 2024, Q16

questions.prompt:
1 pen and 1 notebook cost $\pounds 3.60$
1 pen and 4 notebooks cost $\pounds 9.90$

Work out the total cost of 5 pens and 2 notebooks.
You must show all your working.
hints: Compare the two lines: what is different between them?
The difference in cost is caused only by the extra items.
Once you know one price, use the first line to find the other.
questions.solution:
Difference: $3$ notebooks cost $\pounds 9.90 - \pounds 3.60 = \pounds 6.30$ [P1]
1 notebook $= \pounds 6.30 \div 3 = \pounds 2.10$ [P1]
1 pen $= \pounds 3.60 - \pounds 2.10 = \pounds 1.50$ [P1]
Total: $5 \times \pounds 1.50 + 2 \times \pounds 2.10 = \pounds 7.50 + \pounds 4.20 = \pounds 11.70$ [P1 A1]
questions.inspiredBy: Edexcel GCSE Maths Foundation Paper 1 (Non-Calculator), November 2024, Q16

questions.prompt:
1 adult ticket and 1 child ticket cost $\pounds 13.00$
3 adult tickets and 1 child ticket cost $\pounds 31.00$

Work out the total cost of 2 adult tickets and 4 child tickets.
You must show all your working.
hints: Compare the two lines: what is different between them?
The difference in cost is caused only by the extra items.
Once you know one price, use the first line to find the other.
questions.solution:
Difference: $2$ adult tickets cost $\pounds 31.00 - \pounds 13.00 = \pounds 18.00$ [P1]
1 adult ticket $= \pounds 18.00 \div 2 = \pounds 9.00$ [P1]
1 child ticket $= \pounds 13.00 - \pounds 9.00 = \pounds 4.00$ [P1]
Total: $2 \times \pounds 9.00 + 4 \times \pounds 4.00 = \pounds 18.00 + \pounds 16.00 = \pounds 34.00$ [P1 A1]

questions.prompt:
240 tickets are sold for a concert.
75% of the tickets are child tickets. The rest of the tickets are adult tickets.
The total cost of the 240 tickets is £2340
Each child ticket costs £6.00
Work out the cost of each adult ticket. (4)
hints: Find the number of child tickets and their total cost first.
questions.solution:
Child tickets: $75\%$ of $240 = 180$ [M1]
Child cost: $180 \times 6 = 1080$ [M1]
Adult tickets: $60$, costing $2340 - 1080 = 1260$ [M1]
Each adult ticket $= 1260 \div 60 = \pounds 21.00$ [A1]

questions.prompt:
Harry works in a shop.
From Monday to Friday the basic rate of pay is £9.50 per hour.
On Saturday and Sunday, the rate of pay is $1\frac{1}{2}$ times the basic rate of pay.
The table shows the number of hours Harry worked each day last week.
Work out Harry's total pay last week. (4)
hints: Add up the weekday hours and the weekend hours separately.
questions.solution:
Weekday hours: 27, pay $27 \times 9.50 = 256.50$ [M1]
Weekend rate: $9.50 \times 1.5 = 14.25$ [M1]
Weekend pay: $7 \times 14.25 = 99.75$ [M1]
Total $= \pounds 356.25$ [A1]

The graph shows the distance, $d$ km, of a car from home at time $t$ hours.

What does the gradient of this graph represent?
hints: Look at the units on each axis: what is (vertical unit) per (horizontal unit)?
questions.solution:
Model answer: The speed of the car (in km per hour). [B1]

The gradient is change in distance $\div$ change in time, which is speed: $200 \div 5 = 40$ km/h.

Here are two number machines.

(a) Find the output of Machine A when the input is $14$. (2)

(b) For Machine B, when the input is $12$, the output is $7$.
Complete Machine B by filling in the missing operation. (2)
hints: For (a), do each box in order from left to right.
For (b), work backwards from the output using the inverse operation.
Once you know the number between the boxes, compare it with the input.
questions.solution:
(a) $14 - 3 = 11$, $11 \times 2 = 22$ [M1 A1]

(b) Work backwards from the output: $7 \times 3 = 21$. To get from $12$ to $21$, add $9$. (Accept $\times 1.75$.) [M1 A1]

questions.prompt:
Here are two number machines.

(a) Find the output of Machine A when the input is $6$. (2)

(b) For Machine B, when the input is $9$, the output is $22$.
Complete Machine B by filling in the missing operation. (2)
hints: For (a), do each box in order from left to right.
For (b), work backwards from the output using the inverse operation.
Once you know the number between the boxes, compare it with the input.
questions.solution:
(a) $6 \times 4 = 24$, $24 + 7 = 31$ [M1 A1]

(b) Work backwards from the output: $22 + 5 = 27$. To get from $9$ to $27$, multiply by $3$. (Accept $+18$.) [M1 A1]

questions.prompt:
Here are two number machines.

(a) Find the output of Machine A when the input is $30$. (2)

(b) For Machine B, when the input is $4$, the output is $30$.
Complete Machine B by filling in the missing operation. (2)
hints: For (a), do each box in order from left to right.
For (b), work backwards from the output using the inverse operation.
Once you know the number between the boxes, compare it with the input.
questions.solution:
(a) $30 \div 2 = 15$, $15 - 6 = 9$ [M1 A1]

(b) Work backwards from the output: $30 \div 5 = 6$. To get from $4$ to $6$, add $2$. (Accept $\times 1.5$.) [M1 A1]

hints: Find two numbers that multiply to $-10$ and add to $3$.
Use them to factorise into two brackets.
questions.solution:
$5$ and $-2$ multiply to $-10$ and add to $3$
$(x + 5)(x - 2) = 0$ [M1 A1]
$x = -5$ or $x = 2$ [A1]

hints: Find two numbers that multiply to $12$ and add to $-7$.
Use them to factorise into two brackets.
questions.solution:
$-3$ and $-4$ multiply to $12$ and add to $-7$
$(x - 3)(x - 4) = 0$ [M1 A1]
$x = 3$ or $x = 4$ [A1]

hints: Find two numbers that multiply to $-21$ and add to $-4$.
Use them to factorise into two brackets.
questions.solution:
$-7$ and $3$ multiply to $-21$ and add to $-4$
$(x - 7)(x + 3) = 0$ [M1 A1]
$x = 7$ or $x = -3$ [A1]

questions.prompt:
Leon wants to make $30$ litres of orange paint.
He is going to mix red paint, yellow paint and white paint in the ratio $2:3:1$

Leon has

$\quad 11$ litres of red paint
$\quad 15$ litres of yellow paint
$\quad 4$ litres of white paint

Does Leon have enough red paint, yellow paint and white paint to make $30$ litres of orange paint?
You must show how you get your answer.
hints: Add the ratio parts to find how many parts there are altogether.
Divide $30$ by the total number of parts to find one part.
Multiply to find how much of each is needed, then compare with what is available.
questions.solution:
Total parts: $2 + 3 + 1 = 6$
One part: $30 \div 6 = 5$ litres [P1]
red paint: $2 \times 5 = 10$ litres (has $11$)
yellow paint: $3 \times 5 = 15$ litres (has $15$)
white paint: $1 \times 5 = 5$ litres (has $4$) [P1]

No. Leon needs $5$ litres of white paint but only has $4$. [C1]

Does Hana have enough red paint, blue paint and white paint to make $40$ litres of purple paint?

hints: Add the ratio parts to find how many parts there are altogether.
Divide $40$ by the total number of parts to find one part.
Multiply to find how much of each is needed, then compare with what is available.
questions.solution:
Total parts: $3 + 4 + 1 = 8$
One part: $40 \div 8 = 5$ litres [P1]
red paint: $3 \times 5 = 15$ litres (has $16$)
blue paint: $4 \times 5 = 20$ litres (has $22$)
white paint: $1 \times 5 = 5$ litres (has $5$) [P1]

questions.prompt:
Ravi wants to make $18$ litres of fruit punch.
He is going to mix orange juice, apple juice and lemonade in the ratio $2:5:2$

Ravi has

$\quad 5$ litres of orange juice
$\quad 9$ litres of apple juice
$\quad 6$ litres of lemonade

Does Ravi have enough orange juice, apple juice and lemonade to make $18$ litres of fruit punch?
You must show how you get your answer.
hints: Add the ratio parts to find how many parts there are altogether.
Divide $18$ by the total number of parts to find one part.
Multiply to find how much of each is needed, then compare with what is available.
questions.solution:
Total parts: $2 + 5 + 2 = 9$
One part: $18 \div 9 = 2$ litres [P1]
orange juice: $2 \times 2 = 4$ litres (has $5$)
apple juice: $5 \times 2 = 10$ litres (has $9$)
lemonade: $2 \times 2 = 4$ litres (has $6$) [P1]

No. Ravi needs $10$ litres of apple juice but only has $9$. [C1]

questions.inspiredBy: Edexcel GCSE Maths Foundation Paper 2 (Calculator), November 2024, Q22
questions.prompt:
In London, a 180 g Choci bar costs £2.70
In Madrid, a 300 g Choci bar costs 5.1 euros.
The exchange rate is £1 = 1.16 euros.
In which city is the Choci bar the better value for money, London or Madrid?
You must show how you get your answer. (3)
hints: Convert both prices to the same currency.
Then compare the cost of the same mass, e.g. per 100 g.
questions.solution:
Model answer:
Madrid price in pounds: $5.1 \div 1.16 = 4.40$ [M1]
Cost per 100 g: London $1.500$, Madrid $1.466$ [M1]
Madrid is better value, because 100 g costs less there. [C1]
questions.table:
| London | Madrid
Mass | 180 g | 300 g
Price | £2.70 | 5.1 euros

questions.solution:

questions.prompt:

questions.prompt:
Robyn buys a total of 360 pens and pencils, where number of pens : number of pencils = 4 : 5
Robyn pays 8p for each pen and sells each pen for 12p.
Robyn pays 5p for each pencil and sells each pencil for 7p.
Robyn sells all of the pens and pencils.

hints: Use the ratio to find how many pens and how many pencils.
questions.solution:
Pens: $360 \div 9 \times 4 = 160$, pencils $200$ [M1]

Profit $= 1040$p, so $\frac{1040}{2280} \times 100$ [M1]
$= 45.6\%$ [A1]

questions.prompt:

(a) Work out an estimate for the time taken by the car.

(b) Is your answer to part (a) an underestimate or an overestimate?

hints: Round each number to $1$ significant figure first.

(b) Overestimate: the distance was rounded up and the speed was rounded down, so the time is bigger than it should be. [C1]

questions.prompt:
The table shows part of a train timetable between Wigan and Manchester.
(a) How long should the 07 35 train from Wigan take to get to Bolton? (1)
Sam has a job interview in Manchester. Sam takes 9 minutes to walk from home to the station in Hindley, and will take 7 minutes to walk from the station in Manchester to the interview.
Sam needs to be at the interview no later than 09 00
(b) (i) What is the latest time Sam can leave home and be on time for the interview? (3)
The time of the interview is changed. Now Sam has to be there no later than 09 10
(ii) What effect does the change of time have on the latest time Sam can leave home? (1)
hints: Not every train stops at every station: a blank means it doesn't stop.
Work backwards: arrival in Manchester must be at least 7 minutes before the interview.
questions.solution:
(a) 07 35 to 07 59 is 24 minutes [B1]

(b)(i) Must arrive in Manchester by 08 53 [M1]
The latest train from Hindley that arrives by then leaves at 08 12 (arrives 08 49) [M1]
Leave home 9 minutes earlier: 08 03 [A1]

(ii) It has no effect: there is no later train from Hindley that arrives in time, so the latest time is still 08 03. [C1]

questions.inspiredBy: Edexcel GCSE Maths Foundation Paper 3 (Calculator), November 2024, Q10
questions.prompt:
The table shows part of a train timetable between Ilkley and Leeds.
(a) How long should the 07 25 train from Ilkley take to get to Guiseley? (1)
Priya has a job interview in Leeds. Priya takes 5 minutes to walk from home to the station in Ben Rhydding, and will take 12 minutes to walk from the station in Leeds to the interview.
Priya needs to be at the interview no later than 09 00
(b) (i) What is the latest time Priya can leave home and be on time for the interview? (3)
The time of the interview is changed. Now Priya has to be there no later than 09 45
(ii) What effect does the change of time have on the latest time Priya can leave home? (1)
hints: Not every train stops at every station: a blank means it doesn't stop.
Work backwards: arrival in Leeds must be at least 12 minutes before the interview.
questions.solution:
(a) 07 25 to 07 39 is 14 minutes [B1]

(b)(i) Must arrive in Leeds by 08 48 [M1]
The latest train from Ben Rhydding that arrives by then leaves at 07 57 (arrives 08 30) [M1]
Leave home 5 minutes earlier: 07 52 [A1]

(ii) Priya can now leave later, at 08 52 (the 08 57 train from Ben Rhydding now gets there in time). [C1]

questions.prompt:
The table shows part of a train timetable between Chester and Birkenhead.
(a) How long should the 07 30 train from Chester take to get to Hooton? (1)
Leo has a job interview in Birkenhead. Leo takes 4 minutes to walk from home to the station in Bache, and will take 10 minutes to walk from the station in Birkenhead to the interview.
Leo needs to be at the interview no later than 09 00
(b) (i) What is the latest time Leo can leave home and be on time for the interview? (3)
The time of the interview is changed. Now Leo has to be there no later than 09 20
(ii) What effect does the change of time have on the latest time Leo can leave home? (1)
hints: Not every train stops at every station: a blank means it doesn't stop.
Work backwards: arrival in Birkenhead must be at least 10 minutes before the interview.
questions.solution:
(a) 07 30 to 07 42 is 12 minutes [B1]

(b)(i) Must arrive in Birkenhead by 08 50 [M1]
The latest train from Bache that arrives by then leaves at 08 03 (arrives 08 35) [M1]
Leave home 4 minutes earlier: 07 59 [A1]

(ii) It has no effect: there is no later train from Bache that arrives in time, so the latest time is still 07 59. [C1]

questions.prompt:
You can use this graph to change between miles and kilometres.
(a) Change 15 miles into kilometres. (1)
Rob drives 12 miles from one town to another. He then drives 40 kilometres to a third town.
(b) What is the total distance Rob drives? Give your answer in miles. (3)
hints: Read across from miles to the line, then down to kilometres.
Convert the kilometres into miles before adding.
questions.solution:
(a) 15 miles ≈ 24 km [B1]

(b) 40 km ≈ 25 miles (e.g. 40 km = 25 miles, or 8 km = 5 miles) [M1]
Total $= 12 + 25$ [M1]
$\approx 37$ miles [A1]

questions.prompt:
Cuboid A has length $9\text{ cm}$ and width $2\text{ cm}$.
Its volume is $72\text{ cm}^3$.

(a) Work out the height of Cuboid A. (2)

(b) Cuboid B measures $8\text{ cm}$ by $3\text{ cm}$ by $4\text{ cm}$.
Work out the total surface area of Cuboid B. (3)
hints: Volume of a cuboid $=$ length $\times$ width $\times$ height.
For (a), multiply length by width, then divide the volume by that.
For (b), a cuboid has $6$ faces in $3$ matching pairs. Find the area of each different face, then double.
questions.solution:
(a) $9 \times 2 = 18$, so height $= 72 \div 18 = 4\text{ cm}$ [M1 A1]

(b) $2(8\times3) + 2(8\times4) + 2(3\times4) = 48 + 64 + 24 = 136\text{ cm}^2$ [M1 M1 A1]

questions.prompt:
The diagram shows triangle $ABC$. All measurements are in centimetres.
$AC = BC$
The perimeter of the triangle is 36 cm.
Work out the area of the triangle. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place if necessary. (5)
hints: AC = BC gives you an equation in x.
Split the triangle into two right-angled triangles to find the height.
questions.solution:
$2x + 3 = 4x - 7$ [M1]
$x = 5$, so $AC = BC = 13$ and $AB = 10$ [A1]
Half the base $= 5$ [M1]
Height $= \sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = 12$ [M1]
Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 12 = 60.0\text{ cm}^2$ [A1]

questions.prompt:
The diagram shows triangle $ABC$. All measurements are in centimetres.
$AC = BC$
The perimeter of the triangle is 56 cm.
Work out the area of the triangle. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place if necessary. (5)
hints: AC = BC gives you an equation in x.
Split the triangle into two right-angled triangles to find the height.
questions.solution:
$3x - 2 = x + 14$ [M1]
$x = 8$, so $AC = BC = 22$ and $AB = 12$ [A1]
Half the base $= 6$ [M1]

questions.solution:

Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 15.2 = 76.0\text{ cm}^2$ [A1]

questions.prompt:
The table shows the probabilities that a biased dice will land on $1$, $2$, $3$ and $4$.

Priya assumes that the probabilities that the dice will land on $5$ and on $6$ are the same.

Priya rolls the biased dice $400$ times.

(a) Assuming Priya is right, work out an estimate for the number of times the dice will land on $6$. (3)

Priya is wrong.
The probability that the dice will land on $6$ is greater than the probability that it will land on $5$.

(b) How does this information affect your answer to part (a)? (1)
hints: All the probabilities must add up to $1$.
Subtract the known probabilities from $1$, then split what's left equally between the two missing values.
Expected number $=$ probability $\times$ number of trials.
questions.solution:
(a) Known total: $0.15 + 0.20 + 0.25 + 0.10 = 0.70$ [M1]
Remaining: $1 - 0.70 = 0.30$, so each is $0.30 \div 2 = 0.15$ [M1]
Estimate: $0.15 \times 400 = 60$ [A1]

(b) The probability of $6$ is really more than $0.15$, so the number of times should be higher than $60$. [C1]

questions.prompt:
The table shows the probabilities that a biased spinner will land on Blue, Green and Yellow.

Owen assumes that the probabilities that the spinner will land on Red and on White are the same.

Owen spins the biased spinner $300$ times.

(a) Assuming Owen is right, work out an estimate for the number of times the spinner will land on Red. (3)

Owen is wrong.
The probability that the spinner will land on Red is less than the probability that it will land on White.

(b) How does this information affect your answer to part (a)? (1)
hints: All the probabilities must add up to $1$.
Subtract the known probabilities from $1$, then split what's left equally between the two missing values.
Expected number $=$ probability $\times$ number of trials.
questions.solution:
(a) Known total: $0.35 + 0.20 + 0.05 = 0.60$ [M1]
Remaining: $1 - 0.60 = 0.40$, so each is $0.40 \div 2 = 0.20$ [M1]
Estimate: $0.20 \times 300 = 60$ [A1]

(b) The probability of Red is really less than $0.20$, so the number of times should be lower than $60$. [C1]

questions.prompt:
The table shows the probabilities that a biased dice will land on $3$, $4$, $5$ and $6$.

Jess assumes that the probabilities that the dice will land on $1$ and on $2$ are the same.

Jess rolls the biased dice $250$ times.

(a) Assuming Jess is right, work out an estimate for the number of times the dice will land on $1$. (3)

Jess is wrong.
The probability that the dice will land on $1$ is less than the probability that it will land on $2$.

(b) How does this information affect your answer to part (a)? (1)
hints: All the probabilities must add up to $1$.
Subtract the known probabilities from $1$, then split what's left equally between the two missing values.
Expected number $=$ probability $\times$ number of trials.
questions.solution:
(a) Known total: $0.12 + 0.18 + 0.22 + 0.28 = 0.80$ [M1]
Remaining: $1 - 0.80 = 0.20$, so each is $0.20 \div 2 = 0.10$ [M1]
Estimate: $0.10 \times 250 = 25$ [A1]

(b) The probability of $1$ is really less than $0.10$, so the number of times should be lower than $25$. [C1]

questions.prompt:
Aisha has two boxes of sweets, box A and box B.
In box A, there are only 12 red sweets and 28 green sweets. In box B, there are only 8 red sweets and 17 green sweets.
Aisha is going to take at random a sweet from box A and a sweet from box B.
Which box gives Aisha the greater probability of taking a red sweet, box A or box B?
You must show how you get your answer. (3)
hints: P(red) = number of red ÷ total number of sweets in that box.
Compare them as decimals or percentages.
questions.solution:
Model answer:
Box A: $\frac{12}{40} = 0.3$ [M1]
Box B: $\frac{8}{25} = 0.32$ [M1]
Box B gives the greater probability (0.32 > 0.3). [C1]

questions.prompt:
Zara is playing cards. The probability that Zara will win a game of cards is 0.4
Zara plays two games of cards.
(a) Complete the probability tree diagram by filling in the probabilities (a) to (e) in the table. (2)
(b) Work out the probability that Zara does not win either game. (2)
hints: The probabilities on each pair of branches add up to 1.
questions.solution:
(a) Does not win $= 1 - 0.4 = 0.6$ [B1]
Game 2 branches are the same as game 1: wins $0.4$, does not win $0.6$ [B1]

(b) $0.6 \times 0.6$ [M1]
$= 0.36$ [A1]

questions.inspiredBy: Edexcel GCSE Maths Foundation Paper 3 (Calculator), November 2024, Q15
questions.prompt:
The table gives information about the ages of the 38 children in Westhill football club.
(a) Work out the mean age. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place. (3)
Rohan says, "The highest frequency is 12, so the modal age is 12"
(b) Is Rohan's answer correct? Give a reason for your answer. (1)
hints: Mean = total of (age × frequency) ÷ total frequency.
The mode is the age, not the frequency.
questions.solution:
(a) Age × frequency: 7×5 + 8×9 + 9×12 + 10×8 + 11×4 $= 339$ [M1]
$339 \div 38 = 8.9211\ldots$ [M1]
$= 8.9$ years [A1]

(b) No: 12 is the frequency. The modal age is 9, the age with the highest frequency. [C1]

questions.inspiredBy: Edexcel GCSE Maths Foundation Paper 3 (Calculator), November 2024, Q22
questions.prompt:
The stem and leaf diagram shows the test scores of 23 students from School A. Key: 2 | 5 represents 25
23 students from School B did the same test. Their median score was 52 and the range of their scores was 38
Compare the distribution of the test scores of the students from School A with the distribution of the test scores of the students from School B. (4)
hints: Find the median of School A: with 23 values it's the 12th.
Range = highest − lowest. Compare an average and a spread, in context.
questions.solution:
Model answer:
School A median $= 48$ (the 12th score) [M1]
School A range $= 70 - 25 = 45$ [M1]
School A's median (48) is lower than School B's (52), so on average School A did less well. [C1]
School A's range (45) is bigger than School B's (38), so School A's scores were more spread out, so less consistent. [C1]

questions.prompt:
$400$ students were asked which sport they liked best.

$220$ of the $400$ students were boys.
$90$ of the boys said they liked football best.
$50$ of the girls said they liked tennis best.

$140$ of the students said they liked football best.
$130$ of the students said they liked swimming best.

(a) Complete the two-way table below. (3)

One of these $400$ people is chosen at random.

(b) Find the probability that this person is a girl who said she liked swimming best. (2)
hints: Start with the totals: the two rows must add to the grand total, and so must the three columns.
Fill in any cell where you know all but one value in its row or column.
For (b), read the single cell from the table and put it over the grand total.
questions.solution:
(a) Girls $= 400 - 220 = 180$. Tennis total $= 400 - 140 - 130 = 130$. [B1]
Girls football $= 140 - 90 = 50$. Boys tennis $= 130 - 50 = 80$. [B1]
Girls swimming $= 180 - 50 - 50 = 80$. Boys swimming $= 130 - 80 = 50$. [B1]

(b) $\dfrac{80}{400} = \dfrac{1}{5}$ (any equivalent fraction, decimal or percentage) [M1 A1]

questions.prompt:
$200$ people were asked which fruit they liked best.

$90$ of the $200$ people were women.
$35$ of the women said they liked bananas best.
$25$ of the men said they liked oranges best.

$70$ of the people said they liked apples best.
$60$ of the people said they liked oranges best.

(a) Complete the two-way table below. (3)

One of these $200$ people is chosen at random.

(b) Find the probability that this person is a man who said he liked apples best. (2)
hints: Start with the totals: the two rows must add to the grand total, and so must the three columns.
Fill in any cell where you know all but one value in its row or column.
For (b), read the single cell from the table and put it over the grand total.
questions.solution:
(a) Men $= 200 - 90 = 110$. Banana total $= 200 - 70 - 60 = 70$. [B1]
Men banana $= 70 - 35 = 35$. Women orange $= 60 - 25 = 35$. [B1]
Women apple $= 90 - 35 - 35 = 20$. Men apple $= 70 - 20 = 50$. [B1]

(b) $\dfrac{50}{200} = \dfrac{1}{4}$ (any equivalent fraction, decimal or percentage) [M1 A1]
questions.inspiredBy: Edexcel GCSE Maths Foundation Paper 1 (Non-Calculator), November 2024, Q11

questions.prompt:
$600$ visitors to a museum were asked which gallery they liked best.

$350$ of the $600$ visitors were children.
$150$ of the children said they liked the dinosaurs gallery best.
$40$ of the adults said they liked the space gallery best.

$200$ of the visitors said they liked the dinosaurs gallery best.
$180$ of the visitors said they liked the art gallery best.

(a) Complete the two-way table below. (3)

One of these $600$ people is chosen at random.

(b) Find the probability that this person is a child who said they liked the space gallery best. (2)
hints: Start with the totals: the two rows must add to the grand total, and so must the three columns.
Fill in any cell where you know all but one value in its row or column.
For (b), read the single cell from the table and put it over the grand total.
questions.solution:
(a) Adults $= 600 - 350 = 250$. Space total $= 600 - 200 - 180 = 220$. [B1]
Adults dinosaurs $= 200 - 150 = 50$. Children space $= 220 - 40 = 180$. [B1]
